findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Overall audit assurance has declined: only 80% of audits rated Significant or Reasonable (down from 86% prior year).
findings.detail: The proportion of audits rated Significant or Reasonable assurance has fallen from 86% in 2024/25 to 80% in 2025/26. Although the council notes different services are audited each year, this is a measurable decline in the overall control environment. Multiple audits of housing-related functions received Limited or No Assurance ratings.
findings.matters: A declining proportion of audits providing strong assurance indicates a weakening control environment. For a lender, this signals that governance is deteriorating across the council.
findings.figures: 80% Significant/Reasonable assurance (2025/26) vs 86% (2024/25); 31% Significant vs 49% Reasonable
findings.quote: The percentage of 'Significant' and 'Reasonable' assurance rated audits has slightly declined since last year (80% compared to 86%).

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Housing ICT systems remain weak more than five years after the 2020 cyber attack.
findings.detail: The integrated housing ICT system, which was damaged in the October 2020 cyber attack, is still being implemented post-attack. This delay is actively impacting core housing services including housing management, income collection, leaseholder debt reporting, repairs reporting, and homeless prevention. The council notes recruitment for implementation has progressed more slowly than anticipated.
findings.matters: Weak ICT controls over housing systems undermine the council's ability to manage HRA operations, collect income, and monitor the housing stock. This directly impacts the reliability of HRA financial and operational data.
findings.figures: Still in implementation phase over 5+ years post-attack; multiple service areas affected
findings.quote: In particular, the delay in delivering a fully integrated housing ICT system is impacting some services, particularly housing services, income collection, leaseholder debt, reporting on housing repairs and homeless prevention.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspent by £17.3m due to sharp increase in placements and rising costs.
findings.detail: The council forecast a £17.3m overspend on temporary accommodation for the year, primarily driven by a sharp increase in the number of people placed in temporary accommodation and rising per-unit costs. Although the rate of increase has slowed, this remains a material budget pressure. A Homelessness and TA Transformation Board is in place but the overspend continues.
findings.matters: This is a material forecast overspend driven by demand that the council is struggling to control. For a lender, it indicates both financial pressure and underlying housing market stress in the borough that may persist.
findings.figures: £17.3m forecast overspend for the year
findings.quote: Demand continues to rise for temporary accommodation. Although the rate of increase has slowed compared to the start of the year, a £17.3m overspend is forecast for the year. The overspend is primarily driven by a sharp increase in the number of people placed in temporary accommodation and rising costs.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Leaseholder Major Works Debt Recovery received the worst possible audit rating: No Assurance.
findings.detail: The audit of leaseholder major works debt recovery was rated 'No Assurance' with 4 high priority findings identified. This is the lowest assurance rating, indicating significant weaknesses in the design and operation of controls that could materially impact key system objectives. Leaseholder debt recovery is a material income stream for the HRA.
findings.matters: A No Assurance rating indicates material control deficiencies in a key income function. For a lender, this raises questions about the reliability of HRA income forecasts and the council's ability to collect leaseholder charges.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: Housing repairs overspent by £10.1m (20% of budget) with rising legal and disrepair costs.
findings.detail: Property services forecast an overspend of £10.1m against a £50.8m budget as of February 2026. The overspend is driven by a backlog of repairs (partly pandemic-related) and a significant increase in housing disrepair cases involving damp and mould. Legal costs are forecast to rise significantly as more cases progress through courts for settlement. The council acknowledges the overspend was not forecast through regular budget management, indicating a control weakness.
findings.matters: This is a material forecast overspend on a key operational service. It signals both budget management weakness and a growing liability exposure (disrepair cases and legal costs). The HRA is under financial pressure and this overspend directly erodes reserves.
findings.figures: £10.1m overspend against £50.8m budget (20%); HRA reserves being depleted
findings.quote: The forecast outturn position to budget within property services as at February 2026 is an overspend of £10.1m against the budget of £50.8m. While the increase in, and nature of repair jobs will go some way to explain the overspend, the fact that this was not forecast through regular budget management highlights insufficient focus in this area and the need for improvement.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report June 2026
findings.headline: High priority audit recommendations are not being implemented: only 45% fully implemented against a 90% target.
findings.detail: The council agreed to implement high priority audit recommendations by specified timescales. As of end of March 2026, only 45% were fully implemented and a further 45% partially implemented. This means half of the council's acknowledged control improvements are not being delivered. The report notes this falls well short of the 90% target for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Failure to implement high-priority audit findings leaves identified control gaps open across the council. For a lender, this signals that management is not executing on agreed remedial actions to strengthen controls.
findings.figures: 45% fully implemented, 45% partially implemented, 0% not implemented; target 90% by agreed date
findings.quote: The target for 2025/26 is for 90% of high priority recommendations to be implemented by the agreed timescale. However the percentage currently stands at 45% fully implemented and 45% partially implemented.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - LB Hackney 2024-25 Forvis Mazars Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £19m will remain frozen until statutory override expires at end of 2026, creating further general fund pressure
findings.detail: The council reported a net DSG deficit balance of £16.4m as at 31 March 2025 (£19m gross deficit offset by £2.6m credit reserve). The statutory override allowing this has been extended but is due to end in 2026. If the override is not extended, the council will be forced to begin repaying this deficit from the general fund, placing further pressure on a reserve that is already being depleted at £43.5m per year.
findings.matters: A fixed deadline for the removal of the DSG override creates a known financial cliff. If the override is not extended, the council's already-constrained general fund will face an additional charge, either reducing services or depleting reserves faster.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £19.080m at 31 March 2024, forecast to remain at this level until 31 March 2026; net DSG balance £16.4m; statutory override due to end 2026
findings.quote: We also note that should the statutory override for the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG), due to end in 2026, not be extended, further pressure may be placed on the General Fund as the Council's DSG deficit at 31 March 2024 was £19.080m and is forecast to remain at this level until 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - LB Hackney 2024-25 Forvis Mazars Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing gave council a 'C3' grading for serious failings in safety and quality standards; Housing Ombudsman found repeated service failures in repairs, complaints handling, and data management
findings.detail: The auditor has identified a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness, specifically relating to social housing governance. The Regulator of Social Housing gave a 'C3' grading indicating serious failings in delivering consumer standards and a need for significant improvement. The Housing Ombudsman's special investigation (May 2025) found wider repeated service failures in repairs and maintenance, mould and damp, complaints handling, and knowledge/information management, with underlying problems in scrutiny and oversight. The council referred itself to the Regulator twice — once in June 2024 and again by end of June 2025 for non-compliance.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure in social housing puts a council at reputational risk and suggests management and oversight weaknesses. The audit report explicitly flags that the council has failed to make sufficient progress against the regulator's recommendations, which is a governance red flag.
findings.figures: C3 grading from Regulator of Social Housing; 33% of recorded repairs visits are repeats; council self-referred twice within 12 months
findings.quote: In response to regulatory scrutiny, the Council self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) in June 2024 for non-compliance with the new Safety & Quality Tenant Satisfaction Measure, resulting in a 'C3' grading. This indicates serious failings in delivering consumer standards and a need for significant improvement... The council subsequently referred itself to the Regulator again for not having fully met their expectations in the abovementioned areas by the end of June 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - LB Hackney 2024-25 Forvis Mazars Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £13.6m in 2024/25 with budget growth of £21.3m for 2025/26, despite operating core financial systems on Google spreadsheets
findings.detail: Temporary Accommodation is a major financial pressure, representing £13.6m of the total £18.2m overspend in the Climate, Homes and Economy service. The council plans budget growth of £21.3m in 2025/26 alone, rising to £33.8m by 2028/29. Internal Audit identified that the TA team has worked from Google spreadsheets since a 2020 cyber-attack, with a booking system upgraded in June 2025 but the finance function still relying on spreadsheets until an integrated system is available in 2027. This creates documented risks of payment errors, late billing, arrears, and inefficient resource use.
findings.matters: A council's temporary accommodation service is hard to control — it is driven by homelessness demand — but operating core financial systems on spreadsheets creates avoidable overspends and loss of control. A lender needs to know whether apparent overspends are due to demand or mismanagement.
findings.figures: TA overspend 2024/25: £13.6m (of £18.2m total service overspend); budget growth 2025/26 £21.3m, rising to £33.8m by 2028/29; July 2025 monitoring showed £2.056m underspend but vulnerable to demand shifts
findings.quote: The TA service incurred an overspend of £13m for 2024/25. As part of the 2025/26 budget, the total growth was £21.3m, rising to £33.8m in 2028-29... Following a major cyber-attack in 2020, the Council's Temporary Accommodation (TA) team have been working from google spreadsheets rather than a booking system... the finance function will continue to rely on spreadsheets until the integrated NEC housing system is made available which is not expected until 2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - LB Hackney 2024-25 Forvis Mazars Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand surge (40% increase in clients since 2019) driving uncontrolled cost growth, compounded by London Living Wage inflation
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is the council's largest cost driver of overspend. Clients have increased 40% since 2019/20, and homecare demand has increased over 73%. These volume increases are compounded by escalating unit costs due to inflation, including the London Living Wage (LLW) requirement, and complexity of care packages. The council has achieved only £2m of cost reductions/efficiencies in 2024/25 and is attempting to manage through fee uplift strategies and a transformation programme.
findings.matters: Demographic and wage-driven cost pressures on adult social care are not discretionary and hard to control. Unchecked demand growth threatens the financial sustainability of any council, but particularly one with high deprivation and limited reserves.
findings.figures: 40% increase in Adult Social Care clients since 2019/20; homecare demand increased by over 73%; £2m of cost reductions achieved in 2024/25
findings.quote: There has been a 40% increase in clients since 2019/20. Homecare demand has increased by over 73% to the date of the Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) presented on 24 February 2025. This increased demand has been compounded by escalating unit costs due to inflation, including the London Living Wage (LLW), and the complexity of care packages.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - LB Hackney 2024-25 Forvis Mazars Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Unsustainable reliance on reserves to bridge structural budget gaps, with acknowledged risk that transformation savings may not be delivered
findings.detail: The auditor has identified a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for financial sustainability. Despite a multi-year transformation savings plan, the council continues to rely on reserve depletion to balance budgets. The MTFS shows budget gaps of £17.7m (2026/27), £21.7m (2027/28), and £30m (2028/29) even after transformation savings. Without those savings, gaps rise to £51m by 2028/29. The council plans to drawdown £15–20m of reserves to balance 2025/26 alone.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver sustained savings and dependent on one-time reserve depletion is not financially sustainable and poses credit risk. The auditor has explicitly flagged this as a significant weakness in governance.
findings.figures: Budget gaps after transformation savings: 2026/27 £17.7m, 2027/28 £21.7m, 2028/29 £30m; without transformation savings £51m by 2028/29; 2025/26 planned reserve drawdown £15–20m
findings.quote: Continued reliance on the use of reserves to mitigate lack of savings delivery and bridge budget gaps is unsustainable and risks the Council depleting its reserves whilst not achieving the savings and cost control measures needed to deliver services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - LB Hackney 2024-25 Forvis Mazars Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: General fund reserves will be exhausted within two financial years at current spending levels
findings.detail: The council's general fund reserve balance has fallen from £154.1m at 31 March 2024 to £111.6m by 31 March 2025, a reduction of £43.5m in a single year. The council has determined it has sufficient reserves to cover expenditure at current levels for approximately two financial years to March 2027 before these are exhausted. The 2024/25 £26.3m revenue overspend was wholly balanced by drawdown of reserves.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to know when a council will run out of reserves and be unable to meet unforeseen costs. With only two years of runway, the council faces severe financial distress if savings targets slip.
findings.figures: General fund reserve fell from £154.1m (31/03/2024) to £111.6m (31/03/2025); sufficient reserves to cover expenditure for approximately two financial years to March 2027
findings.quote: The Council has determined that it has sufficient reserves to cover expenditure at current levels for approximately two financial years to March 2027 before these are exhausted.

findings.headline: Climate scenario analysis identifies plausible downside scenario that would threaten fund solvency
findings.detail: The fund conducted climate stress testing and narrative scenario analysis. Under the 'Climate Catastrophe' pathway (delayed policy response to climate events), the report states: 'There is therefore a plausible downside scenario prompted by a climate-related event that would put the Fund's funding strategy at risk.' This is identified as a risk to be monitored.
findings.matters: Long-dated pension liabilities and equity-heavy asset allocation (36% overseas equity, 20% private lending) expose the fund to climate-related economic disruption. This is a tail risk that could force rapid contribution or strategy changes.

findings.paper_title: PC 30 March 2026 Appendix 1 LBH Pension Fund 2025 Triennial Valuation Report DRAFT (1)
findings.headline: Funding level highly sensitive to inflation: each 0.1% higher inflation reduces it by ~2% (£22m)
findings.detail: The report explicitly models inflation sensitivity: if future CPI inflation is 0.1pp higher than the 2.3% assumption, the funding level would fall by approximately 2% (with a £22m fall in surplus). Given that inflation ran 3.4pp above expectation in the inter-valuation period, this is material risk.
findings.matters: This shows the fund's strategy is fragile to inflation. If inflationary pressures persist or UK policy tightens further, the pension fund's comfortable surplus could erode rapidly, forcing contribution increases.

findings.paper_title: PC 30 March 2026 Appendix 1 LBH Pension Fund 2025 Triennial Valuation Report DRAFT (1)
findings.headline: Contribution rates falling but depend on achieving 6.4% investment returns, and prudence has been raised
findings.detail: Hackney's primary contribution rate fell from 20.4% to 16.5%, and secondary rates declined from 6.2% to between 4.0-6.9%. However, this is contingent on the fund achieving 6.4% annual returns with only 80% confidence. The fund explicitly states it has increased prudence levels to reflect geopolitical tensions and financial market volatility, despite the improved funding position.
findings.matters: Lower contribution rates improve affordability for the council short-term, but are built on assumptions about returns that have been unreliable. If returns disappoint again, or geopolitical risks materialise, rates will have to rise.
findings.figures: Primary rate 16.5% (down from 20.4%); secondary rate 2026/27 6.9% (down from 6.2%); discount rate 6.4% at 80% likelihood
findings.quote: On average, employer total contribution rates (ie Primary plus Secondary) have reduced mainly due to higher assumed future investment returns at 2025 compared to 2022. However, there is also increased uncertainty within the wider environment due to ongoing geo-political tensions and financial market volatility, alongside additional uncertainty about future long-term UK inflation levels and global financial markets. Therefore, the Fund has increased the level of prudence within funding strategies and contribution rates at the 2025 valuation.

findings.matters: High inflation reduces funding levels and increases future liabilities. A finance director needs to know that recent experience suggests wage and inflation pressures will persist, which could drive future contribution increases despite current lower rates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Business cases lack transparency on upfront costs, and several 'invest-to-save' proposals cannot be properly scrutinised without detailed financial modelling
findings.detail: Panel states it is difficult to make judgements without sight of business cases underpinning high-level figures. For 18 September Children & Education proposals, Panel notes 'it was disappointing that no figures (one-off or recurrent) were presented in the report on the financial investment needed to achieve the suggested reduction in demand' and specifically queries whether savings figures from pilot programmes are realistic. Panel requests data backing proposals be presented at proposal stage or proposals postponed.
findings.matters: Lack of transparency around upfront investment costs and delivery mechanics means actual net impact is opaque. Proposals could deliver less benefit than claimed if hidden costs are substantial.
findings.figures: Examples: SEND Transformation £2.619m; Looked After Children £2.356m; Fostering Service £2.529m—all with investment costs not fully specified
findings.quote: We request that in future the data backing up proposals needs to always be presented at the proposal stage otherwise that proposal needs to be postponed. Concern was expressed too about a lack of clarity at times regarding upfront costs and the short-term net impact of proposals, relating for example to investment and redundancy costs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Pension fund employer contribution reduced by 6% in single evaluation period, creating reverse-underwriting risk if market conditions deteriorate
findings.detail: Panel notes major concerns about the significant 6% drop in employer contribution percentage within a single actuarial evaluation. Panel worries about potential risks to the pension fund and the council's capacity to reverse this decision and increase contributions before the next 3-year re-evaluation should unforeseen circumstances arise. If investment returns fall, contributions would need to increase sharply.
findings.matters: Pension gains assumed in projections are contingent on continued strong asset returns. A market downturn could force sudden, large increases in employer contributions, creating mid-year budget shock.
findings.figures: 6% drop in employer contribution percentage (FCR1/HRA1 - £4.818m saving)
findings.quote: major concerns remain regarding the significant drop of 6% in employer contribution percentage within a single evaluation period. Panel Members are worried about the potential risks to the Pension Fund and the Council's capacity to reverse this decision and increase contributions before the next 3 year re-evaluation, should unforeseen circumstances arise.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Historical underachievement of savings targets in Children & Education, Climate Homes and Economy, and Finance means delivery assumptions are optimistic
findings.detail: Panel explicitly flags concern about historical track record of achievement of savings targets particularly in C&E, CHE and F&CR. Whilst officers note that most savings have been delivered overall, there have been particular challenges in CHE this year due to issues like vandalism and behaviour change. Savings impacting frontline services can face delays. Panel requests regular updates on what actions are being taken when targets are repeatedly missed.
findings.matters: If high-risk directorates under-deliver again, the £51m gap widens and forces emergency cuts mid-year or accelerates EFS need.
findings.figures: No specific figures, but impacts multiple directorates across 3-year period
findings.quote: There is a concern here that there was a significant increase in temporary accommodation last year and we have little resilience for further shocks. Officers acknowledged that there is always risk in the assumptions made for the medium-term financial plan due to factors such as demand for services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation costs overran significantly last year with little resilience for further shocks
findings.detail: Panel notes there was a significant increase in temporary accommodation last year and expresses concern that there is very little resilience for further shocks. Homelessness prevention proposal of £3m is ambitious given the history of cost pressures in this area. Multiple external variables (government policy, housing market, economy) are outside council control.
findings.matters: A high-volatility demand area with overspend track record and external drivers. Future overspends could exhaust reserves faster than projected.
findings.figures: Homelessness budget growth £21.3m (2025/26 assumption); TA savings proposal £3m
findings.quote: There is a concern here that there was a significant increase in temporary accommodation last year and we have little resilience for further shocks.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: £19m SEND overspend is being addressed via balance-sheet accounting treatment from reserves rather than sustainable cash reduction
findings.detail: Panel notes that relying on balance sheet treatment of the SEND overspend is not a sustainable long-term solution and has flagged this concern nationally. Cash flow implications of this policy will need to be addressed. The council is using reserves to book a provision rather than delivering actual service cost reductions, which defers the problem rather than solving it.
findings.matters: Accounting treatment masks a real cash deficit. When reserves are insufficient to cover this notional provision, the council faces an immediate cash crisis requiring cuts or EFS.
findings.figures: £19m SEND special accounting provision
findings.quote: relying on balance sheet treatment is not a sustainable long-term solution, a point which has very much been flagged nationally. Cash flow implications of this policy will need to be addressed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Annual demand growth in Adults, Children's and Homelessness services has systematically exceeded assumptions every year
findings.detail: Growth assumptions for 2025/26 were £20.9m for ASC, £1.4m for Children's Social Care, and £21.3m for Homelessness. Panel notes these growth assumptions have been surpassed every year. IMPOWER initiative is forecast to deliver £7.4m minimum (potentially £13.1m) to help manage growth, but Panel stresses need for more frequent updates and worries that services lack requisite resources and confidence in their savings being correct.
findings.matters: Systematic growth overruns indicate forecasting model is unfit for purpose and budget risk is actually larger than stated. Lenders cannot rely on council projections.
findings.figures: 2025/26 growth assumptions: £20.9m ASC, £1.4m CSC, £21.3m Homelessness; IMPOWER savings £7.4m minimum rising to £13.1m
findings.quote: The growth assumptions have been surpassed every year. Panel Members would welcome more frequent updates on changes in the growth assumptions and further information to better understand these figures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: £21m of annual transformation savings planned but marked as 'largely unproven in practice' with risk to frontline services if undelivered
findings.detail: Transformation savings are expected to narrow budget gap by £14m in 26/27 then £21m in both 27/28 and 29/28. Panel expresses scepticism about deliverability and notes if these savings are not delivered, gaps will rise markedly. Panel specifically states 'a concern about the weight given to Transformation Savings in the process when it is largely unproven in practice and therefore the risk for the Council is to focus higher savings to be delivered by frontline services.'
findings.matters: A material portion of planned deficit closure rests on savings with no track record, creating significant execution risk and potential for mid-year financial deterioration.
findings.figures: £14m transformation 26/27; £21m each year 27/28 and 28/29
findings.quote: Transformation savings are expected to narrow the budget gap by £14m in 26/27 and then by £21m in both 27/28 and 28/29. The significance of these cannot be overstated as the gaps will rise markedly over the period if the Transformation savings identified are not delivered.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 14 - Budget Scrutiny Report on the Council Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Reserves exhaustion within 1-2 years at current overspend rate, risking Exceptional Financial Support intervention
findings.detail: £10m of non-recurrent reserves were used to balance 2025/26. Panel notes that if the council continues to overspend, reserves will be exhausted within 1-2 years or faster if spending continues to grow. With only £9.2m earmarked reserves forecast at start of 2026/27, the council could face EFS requirement. Panel notes Hackney has prior loss-of-financial-control experience 25 years ago with severe impact on vulnerable residents.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion forces either uncontrolled service cuts or statutory intervention which restricts borrowing and council autonomy—both material credit events.
findings.figures: £10m used 2025/26; £51m projected gap 2026-29; £9.2m earmarked reserves forecast at 2026/27 start
findings.quote: reserves will be exhausted within 1-2 years, or faster, if spending continues to grow. We agree with the Section 151 Officer that the urgency of this needs to take priority as the alternative would be that decisions are taken away from Hackney's elected politicians and residents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £19.1m; inflation and falling rolls pushing more schools into deficit, creating unfunded school closure liability
findings.detail: The DSG reserve is in deficit by £19.1m (eligible for 90% government grant in Autumn 2026 if SEND reform plan approved). More schools are moving into deficit due to inflation and falling rolls. If a school closes due to insufficient pupil numbers, redundancy costs and any remaining school deficit fall on the General Fund.
findings.matters: Schools deficits create an unfunded liability; school closures could trigger additional pressure on already-depleting General Fund reserves beyond current budgeted drawdowns.
findings.figures: £19.1m DSG deficit; 90% government grant cover; more schools now in deficit
findings.quote: The impact of inflation alongside falling rolls has meant that more of our schools are now in deficit. This is a financial risk to the Council as where a school closes, for example, as a result of insufficient pupil numbers the cost of redundancies and any remaining deficit balance are borne by the Council's General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve at £19m (4.5% of budget) is below the historical 5% policy target; S151 officer recommends rebuilding to £22-24m
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Reserve—the ultimate safety net for unexpected costs—sits at £19m, equivalent to 4.5% of the net General Fund budget. The council's historical policy is to hold reserves at around 5% of budget, equivalent to £22-24m. The S151 officer acknowledges the need to rebuild reserves over time but notes this is constrained by current financial pressures.
findings.matters: At 4.5%, the council's unallocated reserves are below policy and below comfort levels for a large metropolitan authority managing high-demand services and significant borrowing.
findings.figures: £19m General Fund Reserve; 4.5% of budget; policy target 5% (£22-24m)
findings.quote: the aim is to increase these to at least 5% of our net revenue budget over time which would equate to £22m - £24m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: £12.6m of required savings depends on delivery of Corporate Transformation Programme; transformation risk flagged as specific concern
findings.detail: The council's savings plans are heavily dependent on £12.6m of savings from a Corporate Transformation Programme, phased as £6.4m in 2026/27, £5.4m in 2027/28, and £0.8m in 2028/29. The S151 officer explicitly flags the delivery risk of this programme as a specific concern for 2026/27, noting the high proportion of total savings that relies on transformation.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver transformation savings would force unplanned reserve drawdowns. This concentration of risk in a single programme accelerates the path to reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £12.6m total transformation savings; £6.4m in 2026/27
findings.quote: For 2026/27 a specific risk is raised concerning the delivery of a significant savings programme which includes around the assumption built into the MTFP regarding the Corporate Transformation Programme. A high proportion of the savings plan £12.6m is built in

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: The MTFP for 2027/28–2029/30 shows a £10m budget gap requiring further savings delivery
findings.detail: Beyond 2026/27, the council faces a known £10m budget gap in the medium-term financial plan. The S151 officer notes this gap must be closed through approved savings plans and new savings proposals. If savings do not materialize, this shortfall will draw down reserves further.
findings.matters: A known future budget gap increases the risk of accelerated reserve depletion if savings plans fail; it signals the financial pressures facing the council are structural rather than temporary.
findings.quote: Attention is drawn in my conclusion to Appendix five of this report which sets out the Medium Term Financial Plan for 2027/28 to 2029/30 within which we estimate a budget gap of £10m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand continues to escalate; council budgets £9.7m additional growth for 2026/27 after £44m in 2025/26
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is the primary driver of the current year overspend. Both the number of people requiring care and the complexity of their needs are rising. The council has built £9.7m of growth into the 2026/27 budget for social care alone, on top of the £44m added for 2025/26, but acknowledges the risk that demand may outstrip this.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-led and non-discretionary; the council cannot control unit costs or service volumes. Persistent overspending despite generous growth suggests demographic and cost drivers are structural, threatening long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £44m growth 2025/26; £9.7m additional growth 2026/27; demand escalating beyond budget
findings.quote: the increase in the number requiring care and support and increasing complex care continues to rise and we are injecting additional growth to respond to this escalating demand.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecasting £8m overspend; HRA reserves fallen below 10% viability minimum and Regulator issued C3 governance grading
findings.detail: The HRA is forecasting an £8m operational overspend driven by escalating reactive repairs and maintenance costs. To cover this the council is drawing £4m from HRA reserves, reducing them below the 10% of turnover minimum required for financial viability. Additionally, the Regulator of Social Housing issued a C3 grading and a Housing Ombudsman investigation found statutory safety checks could not be evidenced.
findings.matters: HRA is self-financed and cannot be bailed out from the General Fund. The combination of operational overspend, regulator concern, and reserve depletion puts housing services at risk and signals control weaknesses.
findings.figures: HRA overspend £8m; reserves drawn to below 10% of turnover threshold; C3 governance rating from Regulator
findings.quote: This year the HRA is forecasting an overspend in its operating activities of £8m which is driven by the increasing spend on reactive repairs and maintenance. This escalating overspend within the HRA is significantly impacting the level of HRA reserves and presents a risk to the financial sustainability and resilience of the HRA and Business Plan going forward.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing surged from £158m to £247m in nine months; debt service costs rising sharply
findings.detail: The council's external borrowing increased by £89m between March and December 2025 to fund capital schemes. The 2026/27 budget adds £4.8m for minimum revenue provision (debt repayment), with MRP costs forecast to rise from 4.1% of the General Fund budget today to 7.5% by 2028/29 as the council pursues a £2bn capital programme.
findings.matters: Escalating debt service costs crowd out revenue spending on services and reduce borrowing capacity. With reserves depleting simultaneously, the council is in a weakened position to manage refinancing risk or interest rate movements.
findings.figures: Borrowing £158m (March 2025) to £247m (December 2025); MRP increase £4.8m in 2026/27; MRP rising from 4.1% to 7.5% of budget by 2028/29
findings.quote: As of March 2025, our long-term borrowings amounted to £158m. This increased to £247m by December 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: The council forecasted £10.3m overspend in 2025/26 despite adding £44m growth specifically for social care and homelessness
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget included £44m of growth to cover cost pressures in Adult Social Care and homelessness prevention, plus a further £10m drawn from reserves. Despite this, the council is still forecasting a £10.3m overall overspend. Adult Social Care is the main driver, with demand for complex care escalating beyond budget.
findings.matters: It demonstrates the council's inability to estimate demand-led service costs accurately; even generous budget growth is insufficient, suggesting structural rather than cyclical cost drivers.
findings.figures: £44m growth budgeted; £10.3m forecast overspend; £10m reserves used
findings.quote: Despite this increased investment in the demand led services the Council is forecasting an overspend of £10.3m. One of the main drivers of the forecast overspend in 2025/26 is Adult Social Care with the increase in the number requiring care and support and increasing complex care continues to rise

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - Section 25 statement 2026_27
findings.headline: If current overspending continues, the council's reserves will be exhausted within 2-3 years
findings.detail: The council's General Fund and earmarked reserves are forecast to decline sharply due to persistent overspending. Reserves have already fallen from £111.6m (March 2025) to forecast £44.9m by end of 2025/26 after the council draws down £10.3m to cover current year overspend. The S151 officer warns that at the current rate of drawdown, reserves will be depleted within 2-3 years.
findings.matters: A council without financial reserves cannot manage demand shocks, unexpected costs, or economic downturns; it becomes dependent on grant support and loses borrowing capacity, constraining a lender's security.
findings.figures: Reserves forecast £44.9m end 2025/26, down from £111.6m March 2025; £10.3m drawn in 2025/26 to cover overspend
findings.quote: if we were to do nothing and we were to continue to overspend at the current rate our reserves will be exhausted within 2 - 3 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Strategy 2026_27 to 2028_29
findings.headline: Council recognises it must remain within revenue affordability despite ambitious capital ambitions, and is undertaking asset challenge to release receipts.
findings.detail: Section 4.6 notes 'the programme does need, however, to remain affordable' and describes an 'Asset Challenge project' to 'perform a formal and systematic challenge and review process for the estate to ensure only those assets needed for the future are retained.' Surplus assets identified 'generating capital receipts and reducing the need for borrowing to finance the capital programme or allocated towards council transformation programmes.' This is a proactive attempt to solve the capital funding gap by disposal.
findings.matters: The council recognises that current borrowing plans strain affordability and is actively looking to sell assets to avoid further debt. Success depends on whether a soft property market will accept disposals at forecast values. If disposals underperform, the council has fewer levers to manage debt.
findings.figures: MRP forecast increase: £8.6m to £43m by 2030/31
findings.quote: As part of the Asset Challenge project the Council will perform a formal and systematic challenge and review process for the estate to ensure only those assets needed for the future are retained and to prioritise investment in assets that deliver and align with the Council's strategic initiatives. This assessment may result in the identification of assets for potential disposal, generating capital receipts and reducing the need for borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Strategy 2026_27 to 2028_29
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery is materially dependent on regeneration scheme viability and organisational capacity amid construction inflation and higher borrowing costs.
findings.detail: Section 5.2 states the capital programme 'will increase in future years though this is materially dependent on viability of our regeneration schemes and organisational capacity and technical skills, and external factors such as construction industry inflation and the increased cost of borrowing.' The council flags this as a constraint on execution, not just on funding.
findings.matters: Even if money is available, the council may not be able to spend it at pace if schemes are unviable or internal delivery capacity is exhausted. Inflation in construction costs erodes value for money on schemes designed years earlier. Higher borrowing costs reduce the net benefit of projects.
findings.quote: The current capital programme suggests this will increase in future years though this is materially dependent on viability of our regeneration schemes and organisational capacity and technical skills, and external factors such as construction industry inflation and the increased cost of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Strategy 2026_27 to 2028_29
findings.headline: Capital programme viability is materially dependent on realising capital receipts from sales amid deteriorating housing market.
findings.detail: The council expects £289m of capital receipts between 2025/26 and 2028/29, 'the majority of this is from sales of properties developed as part of mixed use and housing regeneration schemes.' However, section 8.3 explicitly warns: 'There is also a risk in the modelling, around the volume and value of the capital receipts, taking into account the deterioration in the housing market amid the current economic climate from the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, together with higher inflation and higher interest rates, this will have adverse impact on the housing market. The modelling therefore needs to be revisited on a regular basis.'
findings.matters: If sales volumes or prices fall, the council cannot realise planned receipts to repay forward-funded borrowing. The capital programme would then either slip (delaying benefits) or require permanent additional borrowing. The council already signals this modelling is under strain and needs frequent review.
findings.figures: Forecast capital receipts 2025/26–2028/29: £289m (HRA £144m, GF £145m)
findings.quote: There is also a risk in the modelling, around the volume and value of the capital receipts, taking into account the deterioration in the housing market amid the current economic climate from the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, together with higher inflation and higher interest rates, this will have adverse impact on the housing market. The modelling therefore needs to be revisited on a regular basis.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Strategy 2026_27 to 2028_29
findings.headline: Britannia mixed-use scheme viability at risk from housing market deterioration; shortfalls trigger extra borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The Britannia project (£141m forecast spend 2025/26–2027/28) is primarily funded by sales of private residential units on the site. The council explicitly flags 'considerable work continuing to monitor and manage' the risk because 'Brexit, followed by Covid and current economic events has destabilised the housing market.' Where sales income falls short, 'extra borrowing costs are factored into our medium term financial plan.' A separate project board oversees ongoing financial scrutiny.
findings.matters: Schemes reliant on private residential sales are vulnerable to market swings. Shortfalls force the council to borrow more to backfill gaps, locking in higher long-term debt service. This scheme is material enough to warrant a dedicated governance board.
findings.quote: As this scheme is funded primarily by sale of on-site private residential accommodation there is a significant element of risk. Brexit, followed by Covid and current economic events has destabilised the housing market and there is considerable work continuing to monitor and manage this risk. Where there is a shortfall from the original estimate and therefore a gap in the estimated Council contribution, extra borrowing costs are factored into our medium term financial plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Strategy 2026_27 to 2028_29
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased £90m in nine months (March–December 2025), signalling acceleration in debt take-on.
findings.detail: External borrowing jumped from £158m in March 2025 to £248m by December 2025. This rapid increase reflects front-loaded draw-down on the capital programme to fund mixed-use and regeneration schemes. The council is using 'internal borrowing' (drawing on cash balances) to forward-fund development pending capital receipts.
findings.matters: Rapid debt accumulation tests refinancing capacity and interest rate exposure. The council is not waiting for capital receipts before spending; it is pre-financing schemes and betting on sales to repay the interim debt.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowings: £158m (March 2025) → £248m (December 2025)
findings.quote: As of March 2025, our long-term borrowings amounted to £158m. This increased to £248m by December 2025. We also continue to use internal borrowing, i.e. using balances to temporarily finance capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Capital Strategy 2026_27 to 2028_29
findings.headline: Aggregate Capital Financing Requirement increasing 143% to £1,520m by 2028/29, creating growing revenue pressure.
findings.detail: The CFR (cumulative outstanding debt finance) is forecast to grow from £626m in 2024/25 to £1,520m by 2028/29. Alongside this, the MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision) charge—the annual debt repayment—will increase from £8.6m to £43m by 2030/31, a fivefold increase. This escalating debt service will consume growing shares of the General Fund revenue budget.
findings.matters: For lenders, rapidly accumulating debt represents growing financial risk. For the finance director, MRP charges crowd out spending on services. The council acknowledges it is 'shifting from a low debt position due to significant external borrowing required.'
findings.quote: Current modelling sees the aggregate CFR increase from £626m in 2024/25 to £1,646m in 2028/29. The MRP charge will increase from £8.6m to £43m by 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 Budget Report
findings.headline: Minimum revenue provision (debt repayment) increasing by £4.8m due to growing reliance on borrowing to fund capital programme
findings.detail: The council is raising MRP budgets by £4.8m in 2026/27 to cover principal repayment on a £2,014m four-year capital programme. This reflects a shift from grant-funded to borrowing-funded capital spend and creates a recurring cost liability.
findings.matters: Rising MRP locks in future commitments and crowds out service spending; a lender would scrutinise whether the capital programme is affordable and productive.
findings.figures: £4.8m MRP increase; capital programme £2,014.2m over four years (2026/27-2029/30); largest investment in housing (£1,693.2m)
findings.quote: Increase in the budget for minimum revenue provision as a result of an increased reliance on borrowing to [...] programme (£4.8m).

findings.detail: The council is using the maximum available council tax increase to help balance the budget. This £5.9m contribution is material, indicating limited room for further tax-based funding increases in future years.
findings.matters: High-impact tax increases reduce flexibility and room for manoeuvre in future budgets; a lender would track whether taxpayers can absorb further increases if pressures worsen.

findings.detail: The Mayor's introduction explicitly states the council will need to find an additional £10m in increased income or savings over the four-year MTFP to maintain budget balance. This is not included in the current 2026/27 budget proposals.
findings.matters: A forward-looking structural gap indicates current balance relies on one-off measures or reserves rather than sustainable alignment; a lender would see this as embedded financial stress.

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 Budget Report

findings.detail: The council is budgeting for £9.7m additional spend due to rising demand for both adult social care (£183.3m base) and children's services (£94.7m base). This reflects demographic and policy pressures (homelessness prevention alone is £81.4m, with £64.9m on temporary accommodation).
findings.matters: Social care spend is growing faster than funding; if this £9.7m annual growth persists, structural deficit emerges; a lender would want multi-year visibility of whether this trend will continue.

findings.quote: Assumptions in relation to increases in demand for social care (£9.7m)

findings.paper_title: 2026_27 Budget Report
findings.headline: Concessionary fares budget exceeded by £1.4m (forecast £12.9m vs budget £10.7m) due to surging usage
findings.detail: Concessionary fare costs have risen sharply in recent years and are now forecast to overrun budget significantly. This is a non-discretionary service (free travel for eligible residents) and represents a structural cost driver beyond council control.
findings.matters: A growing unfunded demand pressure in a fixed-cost service signals inability to control spend; a lender would flag this as a permanent upward ratchet on liabilities.
