findings.paper_title: 2026_27 Budget Report
findings.headline: Current-year (2025/26) forecast overspend of £10.249m being absorbed through reserve drawdowns
findings.detail: As of December 2025, the General Fund is tracking £10.249m overspend across multiple services: Children's (£7.575m), Adults/Health (£6.626m), and Housing (£2.005m). The council is managing this by using earmarked reserves (£8.845m allocated to date) but signals budget management stress heading into the new financial year.
findings.matters: Mid-year overspends of this scale indicate forecast or control issues; a lender would question whether management can deliver the savings planned for 2026/27 if current-year controls are not holding.
findings.figures: £10.249m total overspend; Children £7.575m, Adults/Health £6.626m, Housing £2.005m; £8.845m reserves used to offset
findings.quote: Based on Directorate returns, the General Fund forecast for 2025/26 at the end of December[...] an overspend against [the] revenue budget of £10.249m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: Children's services forecasting £1.7m underspend but with acknowledged high volatility risk; new high-need placements could rapidly flip to overspend.
findings.detail: Section 2.2.2 notes Corporate Parenting is 'currently forecasting an underspend of £1.7 million' but explicitly states this 'carries a risk, as it is highly susceptible to variation.' The council notes that placement demand increases during holidays and 'the possibility of new children with particularly complex needs entering the service could quickly add significant costs.'
findings.matters: A forecast underspend in a volatile demand-led service is unreliable and presents downside risk. If complex placements spike, the £1.7m buffer evaporates and creates unexpected pressure on reserves mid-year.
findings.figures: Children's Corporate Parenting forecast underspend 2025/26: £1.7m
findings.quote: Despite these factors, Corporate Parenting is currently forecasting an underspend of £1.7 million... However, this forecast carries a risk, as it is highly susceptible to variation... the possibility of new children with particularly complex needs entering the service could quickly add significant costs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: Transformation programme dependent on capital receipts from asset sales to fund savings initiatives; shortfall would force additional reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: Section 6.3 states the strategy assumes 'we can generate the level of receipts required to fund the strategy.' The council has 'a programme of asset reviews to generate these receipts which will be kept under review.' If asset sales underperform, transformation funding is at risk, forcing further reserve depletion.
findings.matters: A council relying on asset sales (one-off receipts) to fund transformation (recurring savings) creates timing risk and execution dependency. Asset valuations may not materialise; sales take time. If savings don't materialise simultaneously, the council faces a compounding shortfall.
findings.figures: Strategy assumes flexible use of capital receipts to fund transformation; no target receipts figure disclosed
findings.quote: The strategy of using capital receipts flexibly carries an inherent risk: it depends on future receipts from the sale of non-core assets to finance transformation projects aimed at achieving ongoing savings or demand reduction. Should these anticipated receipts not materialise, the associated expenditure would necessitate an increased drawdown on Council reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: Minimum revenue provision (MRP) costs rising steeply: £21.3m (2027/28), £25.9m (2028/29), £31.1m (2029/30), driven by growing dependence on borrowing.
findings.detail: The council forecasts sharp increases in MRP—the provision for repaying capital debt. This reflects a transition from capital receipts (declining) to borrowing to fund capital investment. Section 3.3 notes 'a decreasing pool of capital receipts and a growing dependence on borrowing' requires enhanced revenue provisions. MRP grows 46% between 2027/28 and 2029/30.
findings.matters: Rising MRP locks in growing revenue commitments for years to come. A council shifting from asset sales to borrowing signals assets are depleted. Future revenue flexibility is constrained by past capital decisions.
findings.quote: estimated MRP adds the following amounts to general fund expenditure: 2027/28 £21.287m, 2028/29 £25.935m and 2029/30 £31.068m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: General fund already overspending by £10.3m in 2025/26; £33m of savings required in 2026/27 must be delivered to avoid reserve draw.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 overspend (£10.3m) is already materializing and will be funded from reserves. The council has £33m of approved savings for 2026/27. The financial director notes that 'almost all of the straightforward savings have already been taken,' signalling that remaining savings will require service cuts, not efficiency gains.
findings.matters: An in-year overspend while forecasting 2026/27 deficits demonstrates inability to hold budgets even in years when funding improved. If savings underachieve in 2026/27, the council cannot balance the budget without additional reserves draws.
findings.figures: 2025/26 overspend: £10.3m; 2026/27 required savings: £33m
findings.quote: Reserves will be depleted further by an estimated £10.3m to fund the 2025-26 general fund revenue overspend... Almost all of the straightforward savings have already been taken.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation placements reached 3,749 in December 2025 with 142 net increase annually; council reliant on nightly-paid accommodation; 'structural deficit' between costs and Housing Benefit subsidy.
findings.detail: The council faces persistently increasing homelessness demand. TA placements grew by 142 households annually. Despite allocating £21.3m in 2025/26, the council remains compelled to use expensive nightly-paid temporary accommodation. A structural mismatch between landlord rents and Housing Benefit subsidy rates means the council absorbs losses on every placement. Market rates remain at 'historically high baseline.'
findings.matters: TA is effectively open-ended demand that the council cannot control or refuse. A structural rent-subsidy mismatch means costs will only rise. This is a fiscal ticking bomb: a 3% increase in placements adds significant cost that must come from reserves.
findings.figures: TA placements December 2025: 3,749; annual net increase: 142 households; 2025/26 allocation: £21.300m
findings.quote: persistently increasing demand, evidenced by the number of Temporary Accommodation (TA) placements reaching 3,749 as of December 2025, an annual net increase of 142 households... we remain compelled to utilise nightly paid temporary accommodation... The budgetary impact is further compounded by the structural deficit between landlord rents and the current Housing Benefit subsidy rules.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: Adult social care demand surged 45% since 2019/20; homecare costs up 93%; budget remains under 'considerable strain' despite £26.7m growth allocation by 2029/30.
findings.detail: The council attributes ASC pressure to increased client numbers (45% growth since 2019/20), rising care complexity, and inflationary pressures including London Living Wage. Homecare has grown 93%. Despite allocating £26.7m cumulative growth by 2029/30, the document states the budget 'remains under considerable strain.' Growth keeps rising: £9.7m (2026/27), £16.7m (2027/28), £21.7m (2028/29), £26.7m (2029/30).
findings.matters: Adult social care is the council's largest and least controllable cost. Growth outpacing allocations signals demand management is not working and cost risk is migrating to reserves. Lenders worry when a council cannot control its largest budget area.
findings.figures: ASC client growth since 2019/20: 45%; homecare growth: 93%; cumulative ASC growth allocation 2029/30: £26.7m
findings.quote: the number of individuals receiving care and support has grown by 45%, with homecare alone experiencing a 93% rise... the budget remains under considerable strain.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: Structural budget deficits widening: £3.7m (2027/28), £6.7m (2028/29), £10.2m (2029/30).
findings.detail: The MTFP forecasts growing cumulative budget gaps driven primarily by social care growth allocations, capital charges, and pay awards that outpace revenue growth. The council has already extracted most straightforward savings, requiring transformation to close the £10m gap across the planning period.
findings.matters: Growing structural deficits indicate the council is not balancing on a sustainable basis. A £10m medium-term gap that grows year-on-year signals deepening insolvency risk without major service reductions or income increases.
findings.quote: The cumulative budget gaps are £3.655m in 2027/28, £6.674m in 2028/29 and £10.166m in 2029/30 respectively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5- Medium Term Financial Plan 2027_28 to 2029_30
findings.headline: General fund reserves forecast to be exhausted within 2-3 years at current overspend rates.
findings.detail: Reserves at 31 March 2025 were £111.6m; after deducting committed reserves and other allocations, approximately £44.9m in earmarked reserves remain available. The council forecasts a £10.3m general fund overspend in 2025/26 alone. The financial director warns that if overspending continues at current levels, reserves will be depleted within 2-3 years.
findings.matters: Reserve exhaustion is a critical threshold for lender confidence and council viability. A council facing reserve depletion within 2-3 years signals inability to absorb shocks or service disruptions.
findings.figures: Reserves at start 2025/26: £62.7m; forecast end 2025/26: £30-34m; earmarked reserves: £44.9m; 2025/26 overspend: £10.3m
findings.quote: if we were to do nothing and we were to continue to overspend at the current rate our reserves will be exhausted within 2-3 years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Council diversifying borrowing sources beyond PWLB, including crowdfunding and considering bond issuance
findings.detail: Of the £310m borrowing, £1.05m comes from crowdfunding (Hackney Green Investment initiative). The strategy explicitly states the council 'will investigate the possibility of issuing bonds and similar instruments' and 'will consider long-term loans from other sources including banks, pensions and local authorities' to reduce over-reliance on PWLB.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know if the council can access diverse funding. Crowdfunding for green investment suggests retail investor appetite, but the scale is tiny relative to total need. Bond issuance would signal market confidence or desperation depending on terms achieved.
findings.figures: £1.05m Hackney Green Investment (crowdfunding); total external borrowing £310.05m
findings.quote: The Council has previously and lately raised all of its long-term borrowing from the PWLB but will consider long-term loans from other sources including banks, pensions and local authorities, and will investigate the possibility of issuing bonds and similar instruments, in order to lower interest costs and reduce over-reliance on one source of funding

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Interest rates forecast to fall, reducing near-term borrowing costs but long-term yields expected to remain elevated
findings.detail: Bank Rate expected to reach 3.25% by Q2 2026 (from 4% now), reducing short-term rates. However, long-term gilt yields are expected to remain 'broadly stable on average' and 'higher than in the pre-quantitative tightening era', limiting the benefit for long-term borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender would care about whether borrowing is being done at the right time and rate. The council may face higher long-term borrowing costs than historical precedent, affecting debt affordability.
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast 3.25% by Q2 2026; long-term gilt yields expected to remain elevated and volatile
findings.quote: Long-term gilt yields, and therefore interest rates payable on long-term borrowing, are expected to remain broadly stable on average, though with continued volatility... Yields are likely to stay higher than in the pre-quantitative tightening era

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Council will move from positive cash position to net borrowing requirement of £1,018m by 2029
findings.detail: The council is currently a net lender (holding more cash than external debt), but this position is forecast to reverse sharply. By 2028/29, the cumulative net borrowing requirement reaches £1,018m. This is not unusual for a growing authority, but the speed and scale represent a significant shift in financial posture.
findings.matters: This is a structural shift, not a temporary cash timing issue. A lender needs to understand whether the council's revenue base can support permanent higher debt levels.
findings.figures: Cumulative net borrowing requirement: -£44m (2025, cash positive) → £1,018m (2029, cash negative)
findings.quote: Cumulative Net Borrowing Requirement/ (Investments) -44  171  490  870  1018

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Housing regeneration driving £246m of current borrowing and a significant portion of future capital needs
findings.detail: Of the £310m current external borrowing, £246m is used to finance housing capital programme and regeneration, taken on as part of HRA self-financing in 2012. This indicates the council's regeneration strategy is debt-dependent.
findings.matters: Housing regeneration is typically long-term, lower-return investment. A lender would want to understand the business case, timeline to completion, and whether housing rents will cover debt service or if this is subsidised from general fund.
findings.figures: £246m of £310.05m total external borrowing dedicated to HRA housing capital
findings.quote: £246m long term used to finance part of the borrowing requirement within the HRA reflecting the take on debt as part of the HRA self financing in 2012 and for the financing of the housing capital programme, particularly in respect of housing regeneration

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement growing 143% from £626m to £1,520m over four years
findings.detail: The underlying need to borrow for capital purposes (CFR) is forecast to rise steeply, particularly driven by housing regeneration schemes and broader capital programme delivery. This growth outpaces the council's ability to fund from reserves.
findings.matters: A growing CFR indicates significant capital investment underway. A lender needs to know what this capital is funding (revenue-generating assets, essential replacements, or regeneration with uncertain returns) and whether debt can be serviced from generated income.
findings.quote: the Council has an increasing CFR due to the delivery of its capital programme with many regeneration schemes requiring borrowing upfront ahead of the realisation of capital receipts

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Usable reserves declining from £452m to £332m over the forecast period, forcing shift to external borrowing
findings.detail: The council's balance sheet resources (cash and reserves available for investment and borrowing) are forecast to fall by £120m over four years. This depletion is the stated driver for moving away from internal borrowing (using reserves) towards external borrowing, which creates refinancing and affordability risk.
findings.matters: Falling reserves reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to shocks. A lender needs to understand whether this is manageable decline or a sign of structural imbalance.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources: £452m (31/03/25) → £332m (31/03/29); annual decline of approximately £30m
findings.quote: due to reduced cash balances and increasing capital pressures, the Council is now transitioning towards a more borrowing-led approach

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026_27
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement rising from £882m in 2026/27 to £1,350m cumulative over three years
findings.detail: The council forecasts a net borrowing need of £882m in 2026/27 alone, growing to £1,232m and £1,350m in subsequent years. This represents a major increase from current external borrowing of £310.05m. The growth is driven by capital programme delivery, particularly housing regeneration.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand the council's debt trajectory, capacity to service new debt, and whether the capital programmes delivering this borrowing are revenue-generating or cost-creating.
findings.figures: £882m (2026/27 borrowing requirement); cumulative £1,350m by 2028/29; current external borrowing £310.05m
findings.quote: The balance sheet forecast in Table 2 shows that the Council has a borrowing requirement of £882m in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: Savings proposals of £3.22m identified for 2026/27 but described as having 'none of which creates any tangible reduction in service levels'—indicating shallow reserves of achievable savings
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £3.22m savings (approved in July and September 2025), including triennial pension valuation (£720k), operational efficiencies (£500k), above-inflation fees and charges (£200k), delivery lockers (£100k), new heads of charge to tenants/leaseholders (£1.6m), and rechargeable repairs (£100k). The council explicitly states these 'creates any tangible reduction in service levels,' but the single largest item (£1.6m) is new service charges on tenants, which is effectively cost-shifting not savings.
findings.matters: If the council has exhausted obvious, non-service-reducing savings and still faces structural deficits, future savings are likely to require service cuts or further tenant charges, reducing the HRA's resilience and political sustainability.
findings.figures: £3.22m savings for 2026/27; triennial pension £720k; efficiencies £500k; new tenant charges £1.6m; no tangible service reduction claimed
findings.quote: This has been achieved, in part, through the identification of £3.3m of budget savings within the revenue budget (none of which creates any tangible reduction in service levels).

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: HRA Finance Improvement Board instructed council to 'only order the musts' (legal requirements only) in May 2025, signalling loss of discretionary spending
findings.detail: A newly created HRA Finance Improvement Board gave explicit instruction in May 2025 to limit spend and order only legally required works. Bi-weekly spend review meetings now scrutinise all works. This resulted in a £2.975m reduction in repairs expenditure compared to 2024/25 outturn, but this is driven by rationing discretionary maintenance, not efficiency gains. The existence of this board and its strict spend controls indicate the council recognises the HRA is in financial stress and requires intensive governance oversight.
findings.matters: Discretionary maintenance rationing defers repair costs but worsens long-term asset deterioration, exacerbating the £290m capital funding gap. This signals the council is managing cash crisis rather than addressing structural affordability.
findings.figures: £2.975m reduction in repairs expenditure when compared to 2024/25 outturn; instruction issued May 2025; bi-weekly spend review meetings
findings.quote: The HRA Finance Improvement Board gave an instruction in May 2025 clearly setting out the need to limit spend and only order the 'musts' i.e.the legal requirements.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: 66% of tenants are on benefits; rent collection at risk from cost-of-living pressures and rising arrears
findings.detail: 71% of tenants are in receipt of full or partial housing benefit or universal credit, accounting for just over 60% of rent debit. In receipt of benefits: 15.6% full housing benefit + 4.86% part housing benefit + 50.32% universal credit = 70.78%. The council recognises 'current inflationary pressures on the cost of living for our tenants and leaseholders are imposing severe burdens on all households, particularly poorer residents,' creating risk that 'rent collections rates over the coming year' may be impacted.
findings.matters: With three-quarters of tenants on welfare, rental income is vulnerable to benefit changes and cost-of-living shocks. The council is already implementing tenant sustainability services to mitigate arrears, suggesting arrears are a material risk to HRA cash flow.
findings.figures: 71% of tenants on full or partial housing benefit or universal credit; just over 60% of rent debit from benefits; 50.32% on universal credit; 20.08% on housing benefit
findings.quote: In Hackney, 71% of tenants are in receipt of full or partial housing benefit or universal credit accounting for just over 60% of the rent debit.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: £279m new borrowing requirement over 10 years for regeneration, with capital receipts not realised until after 2033/34
findings.detail: The capital programme requires £279m in new HRA borrowing, predominantly for housing regeneration, estate regeneration, housing supply programmes, and Woodberry Down. However, the capital receipts from sales of private-sale and shared-ownership units are not expected to be realised until after 2033/34, creating a 10+ year timing mismatch. The residual borrowing (approximately 30% of social housing build costs) will be repaid from rental income over 50 years.
findings.matters: Long-dated borrowing repaid from constrained rental income, combined with regulatory concerns (C3 rating) and rising repair costs, increases refinancing risk. Lenders will scrutinise whether rental income can service this debt across 50 years given current trends.
findings.figures: £279m borrowing requirement over 10-year capital programme; capital receipts realised after 2033/34; residual borrowing ~30% of social housing build costs; repayment period 50 years
findings.quote: There is a borrowing requirement over the 10 Year Capital Programme of £279m predominantly to fund the Housing Regeneration Programmes, Estate Regeneration Programme, Housing Supply Programme and Woodberry Down, until capital receipts are realised through sales

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: £290m capital funding gap over 10 years: stock condition surveys reveal the council cannot afford to maintain existing homes to required standards
findings.detail: Stock condition data reveals a significant funding gap. Over 9 years (2025/26–2033/34), the average annual need to invest is £61.824m but available resources are only £44.950m, creating an annual gap of £32.254m (total gap £290.285m). The backlog alone is £138.4m over 9 years. The council is exploring asset disposal and rationalisation but acknowledges 'further meaningful revenue savings are limited.' This gap drives the need for £279m new borrowing over 10 years.
findings.matters: A £290m unfunded capital need means the council cannot maintain homes to meet legal standards (Decent Homes, fire safety, Awaab's Law, energy efficiency). This will result in either further service reductions, higher borrowing, or failure to meet regulatory obligations.
findings.figures: Annual need to invest: £61.824m; Resources available: £44.950m; Annual gap: £32.254m; 9-year gap: £290.285m; Backlog: £138.421m; 10-year borrowing requirement: £279m
findings.quote: The stock condition data reveals a significant funding gap over the current 10 year capital programme, requiring significant resources. Options to bridge this gap will continue to be explored.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: Housing repairs spending is structurally unsustainable, with £9.6m overspend forecast for 2025/26 despite budget increases
findings.detail: The 2024/25 HRA overspend was primarily driven by repairs (reactive repairs, material costs, legal disrepair cases), requiring £7.224m reserve drawdown. Despite significantly increasing the 2025/26 repairs budget, a £9.6m overspend is still forecast. The document states: 'the current level of spend is not sustainable within the HRA MTFS and 30 Year Business Plan.' Reactive repairs costs continue to spiral above CPI due to labour shortages and demand from Awaab's Law compliance.
findings.matters: Repairs are the largest controllable cost in the HRA. If the council cannot bring repair spending within budget despite multiple interventions (spend controls, bi-weekly reviews), this signals a structural affordability problem that threatens financial viability.
findings.figures: 2024/25 overspend: £7.224m; 2025/26 repairs forecast overspend: £9.6m; repair budget increased significantly in 2025/26 but still overrunning
findings.quote: The current financial position and drawdown of earmarked reserves places the HRA budgets under significant financial pressure and the current level of spend is not sustainable within the HRA MTFS and 30 Year Business Plan.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: HRA reserves completely depleted with general reserves falling to 4-7% of turnover, below the prudent 10% minimum
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves of £982k are being completely depleted to balance 2025/26, and a further £2.043m drawdown from general reserves is required. This will reduce general reserves from 8% to between 4-7% of turnover. The council aims to rebuild to 10% by end of 2027/28, but this timeline leaves the HRA exposed to shocks.
findings.matters: General reserves below 10% of turnover indicate reduced financial resilience and ability to absorb unexpected costs or income shortfalls without emergency action.
findings.figures: General reserves currently 8% of turnover; forecast to fall to 4-7% by March 2026; target 10% by March 2028; earmarked reserves £982k drawdown; general reserve drawdown £2.043m
findings.quote: The level of HRA general reserves is currently at 8% of turnover, the removal of the budgeted contribution in 2025/26 and the forecast use of general reserves to balance the HRA in year will result in the general reserve falling to between 4% and 7% as at 31st March 2026.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget Setting 2026_27 Including Rents and Tenant Service Charges - Cabinet Report v1
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing C3 grading for serious failings in tenant satisfaction and consumer standards
findings.detail: The council self-referred to the RSH in June 2024 for non-compliance with the Safety & Quality Tenant Satisfaction Measure, resulting in a C3 grading. The Housing Ombudsman also launched a special investigation into repairs delivery and complaints handling, publishing its final report in May 2025. The council has accepted recommendations and integrated them into an updated Housing Improvement Plan, with quarterly monitoring by HOS.
findings.matters: A C3 rating signals regulatory concern about the council's capacity to manage its housing services and meet statutory obligations, directly affecting lender confidence and the council's ability to borrow.
findings.figures: C3 grading (June 2024); HOS final report (May 2025); Housing Improvement Plan created
findings.quote: the Council self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) in June 2024 for non-compliance with the new Safety & Quality Tenant Satisfaction Measure, resulting in a 'C3' grading. This indicates serious failings in delivering consumer standards and a need for significant improvement.

findings.paper_title: 6a. Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024_25
findings.headline: Recorded liabilities jumped £28.8m due to IFRS16 accounting changes for leases and PFI arrangements.
findings.detail: Other Long Term Liabilities increased from £8.6m to £37.4m, reflecting the first-year implementation of IFRS16 accounting standards for leases and PFI arrangements effective from 2024/25. While this is an accounting change rather than a new financial obligation, it materially changes the council's recorded debt position and must be factored into debt serviceability assessments.
findings.matters: IFRS16 brings off-balance-sheet liabilities onto the balance sheet, increasing recorded debt. Lenders need to ensure they are using consistent debt definitions and understand that the council's total debt position has grown by the full IFRS16 adjustment, not just new borrowing.
findings.figures: Other Long Term Liabilities: £8.581m (31/03/24) to £37.362m (31/03/25); Total External Debt increased from £71.681m to £204.220m
findings.quote: This is a result of the implementation of the IFRS16 regulation concerning leases and PFI arrangements, effective from 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 6a. Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024_25
findings.headline: Capital programme figures are provisional and subject to further review, creating uncertainty in forward projections.
findings.detail: The paper states that 'further review of the capital programme will be happening during the 2024/25 financial year meaning configuration of numbers below are likely to change.' Additionally, accounts remain unaudited at the time of reporting, though the council notes 'no expectation of change.' This introduces execution risk: the ambitious capital programme may not proceed as planned, or costs may shift between years.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on council projections to assess future debt trajectories and revenue impacts. Acknowledging that the capital programme is under review signals uncertainty about the council's financial plans and whether current projections are firm commitments or aspirational.

findings.quote: However further review of the capital programme will be happening during the 2024/25 financial year meaning configuration of numbers below are likely to change.

findings.paper_title: 6a. Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024_25
findings.headline: Council's cash is forecast to decline significantly as major capital schemes progress.
findings.detail: The council's investment balance increased from £39m to £44m during 2024/25, but the treasury outturn explicitly warns that 'The Council is forecasting a downward trend in cash balances as the Council progresses on a number of major capital schemes requiring forward funding.' This signals that available cash will be deployed into capital projects, reducing the liquidity buffer available for operations or contingencies.
findings.matters: Lenders assess liquidity risk alongside borrowing needs. A council drawing down cash reserves to fund capital schemes while increasing debt is consuming its financial buffers, which reduces its resilience to unexpected revenue pressures or capital cost overruns.

findings.quote: The Council is forecasting a downward trend in cash balances as the Council progresses on a number of major capital schemes requiring forward funding.

findings.paper_title: 6a. Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024_25
findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is rising, from 2.2% to 5.0% for non-HRA by 2027/28.
findings.detail: The proportion of the council's revenue budget dedicated to financing costs is increasing. For the non-HRA (general fund), this ratio rises from 2.2% (2024/25) to 3.7% (2025/26), 4.6% (2026/27), and 5.0% (2027/28). For the HRA, the ratio rises to 27.1% in 2025/26 before moderating. This compression of the revenue budget to finance debt is an affordability measure that lenders typically monitor.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and the proportion of revenue available for service delivery. While the trajectory shown is not yet critical, it demonstrates the growing revenue burden of the council's capital ambitions.
findings.figures: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream: Non-HRA 2.2% (2024/25), 3.7% (2025/26), 4.6% (2026/27), 5.0% (2027/28)
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream: Non-HRA 2.2%, 3.7%, 4.6%, 5.0%

findings.paper_title: 6a. Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2024_25
findings.headline: Capital programme is increasingly funded by prudential borrowing, rising from 38% in 2024/25 to 74% by 2027/28.
findings.detail: The council's capital financing breakdown shows prudential borrowing growing from £89m (38% of £232m total spend) in 2024/25 to £327m (64%) in 2025/26, and continuing at 63-74% for subsequent years. Government grants, capital receipts, and other traditional funding sources are insufficient to cover the scale of planned investment.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on prudential borrowing means the council's ability to deliver its capital programme depends entirely on its borrowing capacity and debt serviceability. This is a structural risk if the capital programme cannot be scaled back or funded alternatively.

news_drafts.headline: Overall audit assurance has declined: only 80% of audits rated Significant or Reasonable (down from 86% prior year).

news_drafts.headline: Housing ICT systems remain weak more than five years after the 2020 cyber attack.
news_drafts.lead: Weak ICT controls over housing systems undermine the council's ability to manage HRA operations, collect income, and monitor the housing stock. This directly impacts the reliability of HRA financial and operational data.

news_drafts.headline: Temporary accommodation overspent by £17.3m due to sharp increase in placements and rising costs.
news_drafts.lead: This is a material forecast overspend driven by demand that the council is struggling to control. For a lender, it indicates both financial pressure and underlying housing market stress in the borough that may persist.
